paragraphs: A classifier used by a service provider operates in a market where other providers also compete for customers. This paper studies how that competition changes the learning problem. Its starting point is that prediction accuracy alone does not fully describe what a provider needs to optimize when customers can choose among competing services.

The authors analyze the learning objective in this setting and propose a classification method aimed at maximizing market share in the presence of competitors. This makes the competitive environment part of the learning problem. Their analysis also identifies the timing of market entry and model updates as potentially crucial factors, connecting model development decisions with how the market evolves.

The paper reports benefits for both providers and consumers and demonstrates its approach across settings ranging from simple distributions to noisy datasets. It also finds rapid convergence to an equilibrium in the markets studied. Together, these findings suggest that accounting for competition can improve outcomes while allowing the overall market to settle into a stable state.
icml-2025-a-market-for-accuracy-classifi.tldr: A competition-aware classification method targets market share and reports benefits for providers and consumers alongside rapid market stabilization.

paragraphs: Optimizing several objectives is often treated as a negotiation between competing goals: improving one may require sacrificing another. This paper examines a different setting, where related objectives can improve together. It is motivated by findings in multi-task learning, reinforcement learning, and language-model training that combining related tasks can help performance across objectives simultaneously.

The authors introduce Aligned Multi-Objective Optimization as a framework for studying this situation. The central shift is to make beneficial relationships among objectives part of the optimization problem itself. This addresses a gap between evidence that related tasks can support one another and generic gradient-based methods designed to handle many such objectives.

The paper proposes algorithms for this setting and provides theoretical guarantees of better performance than naive approaches. These guarantees concern the aligned setting introduced by the authors; they do not establish that arbitrary collections of objectives cooperate. The contribution is an optimization framework for situations where improvement across several goals is possible, giving that opportunity a more explicit algorithmic treatment.
icml-2025-aligned-multi-objective-optimi.tldr: The paper develops a framework and theoretically supported algorithms for optimizing many related objectives that can improve together.

paragraphs: Compressing language-model weights to four bits requires choosing which numerical values those bits represent. any4 learns that representation instead of relying on fixed formats such as int4, fp4, or nf4. The method supports arbitrary numerical representations and does not require preprocessing either the model weights or its activations.

Across the evaluated model sizes, generations, and families, including Llama 2, Llama 3, Mistral, and Mixtral, any4 achieves higher accuracy than those other four-bit formats. It is also competitive with AWQ and GPTQ, which involve preprocessing. Experiments with three-bit and two-bit variants report competitive results as well, extending the investigation to more aggressive compression.

The authors also show calibration using one curated, diverse sample instead of the hundreds of dataset samples commonly used by quantization approaches. To support execution, they release tinygemm, a GPU matrix multiplication library optimized for latency. It implements any4 through a GPU-efficient lookup table strategy, connecting the learned numerical format with a concrete implementation for language-model computation.
icml-2025-any4-learned-4-bit-numeric-rep.tldr: any4 learns four-bit weight representations that improve accuracy over fixed formats and supports efficient GPU execution without weight or activation preprocessing.

paragraphs: Controlled generation asks a model to produce samples that satisfy specified requirements. This paper derives an objective for doing so within Variational Flow Matching, which interprets flow matching as a variational inference problem. That perspective gives the authors a common framework for connecting generative modeling with Bayesian reasoning about desired outputs.

The framework supports two routes to control. A conditional generator can be trained end to end, or an existing unconditional generator can be controlled afterward through Bayesian inference without retraining. The paper also establishes conditions for equivariant generation and develops a molecular formulation that respects rotations, translations, and permutations. This addresses the need for molecular generation to handle equivalent spatial descriptions consistently.

In molecular experiments, the approach achieves state-of-the-art results for uncontrolled generation. For controlled generation, it outperforms state-of-the-art models through both end-to-end training and the Bayesian inference route. The stated findings support a shared treatment of control and symmetry, while demonstrating that control can also be applied to unconditional models after training.
icml-2025-controlled-generation-with-equ.tldr: An equivariant Variational Flow Matching framework controls molecular generation through either conditional training or Bayesian inference without retraining.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks learn solutions while encouraging their outputs and gradients to satisfy governing physical equations. The paper identifies a training problem: treating easy and difficult sample locations alike can lead to unstable learning and uneven prediction quality. Physical boundaries are a particular concern because errors can remain concentrated in difficult regions.

CoPINN introduces an easy-to-hard training process inspired by human learning. Its architecture first encodes individual one-dimensional coordinates with separate subnetworks, then combines them to predict multidimensional physical variables. During training, it dynamically estimates each sample's difficulty using gradients of the residuals of the partial differential equation, which measure departures from satisfying the equation.

A training scheduler uses those difficulty estimates to progressively optimize across the sampled regions. This links the order of learning to the model's changing assessment of the problem. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance, with especially substantial error reductions in stubborn regions. The findings support the value of difficulty-aware scheduling for more robust predictions, particularly around physical boundaries.
icml-2025-copinn-cognitive-physics-infor.tldr: CoPINN schedules physics-informed learning from easy to difficult locations, reporting especially strong error reductions in challenging physical regions.

paragraphs: Multi-view classification combines several sources of information about the same instance. Those sources can be noisy or disagree, making confidence as important as the final label. This paper argues that existing evidential approaches can underestimate uncertainty when views conflict because their uncertainty calculations overlook disagreement between the beliefs assigned to different categories.

FUML represents neural-network outputs as fuzzy memberships. It uses both possibility and necessity measures to quantify how credible each category is, then trains those credibility estimates with a tailored loss. An entropy-based method derives uncertainty from category credibility, making the treatment of uncertainty part of the proposed classification framework.

The method also introduces Dual Reliable Multi-view Fusion, which considers uncertainty within each view and conflict between views when combining information. These two signals address distinct sources of unreliability: an individual view may be uncertain, or multiple views may disagree. Experiments report state-of-the-art accuracy and reliability, supporting the combined use of fuzzy credibility estimates and conflict-aware fusion.
icml-2025-deep-fuzzy-multi-view-learning.tldr: FUML combines fuzzy category credibility with uncertainty- and conflict-aware fusion to improve multi-view classification accuracy and reliability.

paragraphs: DIS-CO investigates whether a vision-language model's responses can reveal that copyrighted material appeared in its training data. The motivating hypothesis is that a model can recognize images from its training corpus. This turns recognition behavior into a possible signal of training exposure when the underlying dataset cannot be inspected directly.

The method repeatedly presents selected frames from targeted material and examines free-form text responses for the content's identity. To evaluate this approach, the authors introduce MovieTection: 14,000 film frames with detailed captions. Its films were released both before and after a model's training cutoff, providing a benchmark organized around the question of possible training exposure.

The reported detection performance nearly doubles the best prior method's average AUC on models whose logits are available. The authors also find that every tested model appears to have encountered some copyrighted content. That conclusion remains an inference from model behavior, consistent with the method's recognition hypothesis; the stated finding is apparent exposure rather than direct inspection of training records.
icml-2025-dis-co-discovering-copyrighted.tldr: DIS-CO uses repeated frame-recognition queries to infer possible copyrighted training content and reports stronger detection on a new film benchmark.

paragraphs: Distributing learning across more machines does not always improve training. In decentralized methods, increasing the network beyond a critical size can worsen convergence rates. This paper studies that scalability barrier within stochastic convex optimization, asking how many machines can be used effectively while retaining favorable statistical performance.

The proposed algorithm, Decentralized Anytime SGD, extends the critical parallelism threshold. Its contribution is therefore about the range of useful parallel execution: it aims to let larger machine networks participate without sacrificing the performance guarantees under study. This connects the design of a decentralized learning algorithm directly to the question of how far its computation can be distributed.

The authors establish a theoretical upper bound on parallelism that improves on the existing state of the art. For highly connected network topologies, the result closes the gap with centralized learning. The topology qualification matters to that comparison: the stated centralized-level result concerns highly connected networks. Overall, the paper offers a theoretical route to greater decentralized scalability within the stochastic convex setting.
icml-2025-enhancing-parallelism-in-decen.tldr: Decentralized Anytime SGD expands theoretically supported parallelism and closes the gap with centralized learning in highly connected networks.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning policy can maximize total reward while distributing its benefits unevenly across groups. This paper studies objectives that account for multiple, potentially overlapping groups. One motivating example is maximizing the reward received by the least-rewarded group, which makes the distribution of benefits part of the policy-learning problem.

The authors consider a broader formulation in which each objective reweights a single reward function according to the current state. They provide oracle-efficient algorithms that can handle very large collections of these objectives, including possibly exponentially many constraints over intersecting groups. Oracle efficiency describes the algorithms' use of specified subproblem-solving capabilities, rather than an unrestricted claim about every possible implementation.

The results cover tabular Markov decision processes and large state spaces when the group functions have additional structure. That structural qualification is central to the large-state-space result. Experiments validate the theoretical findings and illustrate applications on a preferential attachment graph environment. The contribution makes a large family of overlapping fairness objectives algorithmically tractable under the stated formulation and conditions.
icml-2025-intersectional-fairness-in-rei.tldr: The paper provides oracle-efficient reinforcement-learning algorithms for possibly exponentially many intersecting-group objectives, with structural conditions for large state spaces.

paragraphs: Models can lose accuracy when deployment data differs from their training data. Test-time training addresses this by adapting during inference, but existing methods often need extra data or a specially designed auxiliary task. IT3 proposes adaptation using only the current test instance and a consistency principle that does not require domain-specific auxiliary-task design.

That principle is idempotence: applying a function again should leave its result unchanged. IT3 adapts the model by reducing the distance between successive applications during inference. The paper theoretically connects this property to prediction confidence, giving a rationale for using repeated-application consistency as the signal that drives adaptation.

Experiments cover image classification, aerodynamics prediction, and aerial segmentation, using architectures including multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and graph neural networks. IT3 consistently outperforms existing approaches in the reported experiments while offering a simpler adaptation setup. The authors interpret these results as evidence that idempotence may provide a broadly applicable adaptation principle; the empirical breadth supports that possibility without establishing success for every domain.
icml-2025-it-3-idempotent-test-time-trai.tldr: IT3 adapts models on a single test instance by encouraging repeated applications to agree, improving performance across several domains and architectures.

paragraphs: Transformer attention lets a model retrieve information from different positions in a sequence. This paper examines the learning signals passing backward through the softmax operation used in standard attention. The authors observe that these gradients can often be small, which can make training less effective for parameters that come before the attention operation.

LASER introduces an attention mechanism with an exponential transformation and analytically establishes a larger gradient signal. The proposed change targets how effectively attention transmits learning information during training. It can be implemented through small modifications to existing attention implementations, making the contribution a focused alteration to a widely used model component.

Experiments on autoregressive language models with up to 7.7 billion parameters report average downstream improvements of up to 1.44% and finetuning improvements of 1.65%. The paper also reports better generalization for vision, speech, and text models, including ViT, Conformer, and a 2.2-billion-parameter BERT. These results connect the gradient analysis to measured improvements across several attention-based architectures.
icml-2025-laser-attention-with-exponenti.tldr: LASER modifies attention to provide a larger gradient signal and reports performance gains across language, vision, and speech tasks.

paragraphs: De novo peptide sequencing reconstructs amino acid sequences directly from tandem mass spectra, without relying on a reference database. A major difficulty is that an observed spectrum may lack fragmentation information because of imperfect fragmentation or instrument constraints. A model that predicts directly from the available spectrum must therefore work with an incomplete account of the peptide.

LIPNovo adds an imputation stage before sequence prediction. It fills in missing information within the model's internal representation rather than synthesizing raw spectral measurements. Guided by the target peptide's theoretical peak profile, it treats the problem as predicting a set: learnable peak queries reason about observed peaks, while optimal bipartite matching associates predicted representations with theoretical peaks.

This design gives the final prediction stage an enriched representation that can supplement missing evidence during inference. Experiments on three benchmark datasets report large improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The stated result supports the paper's central computational choice: reconstruct useful latent information before asking the model to commit to an amino acid sequence.
icml-2025-latent-imputation-before-predi.tldr: LIPNovo reconstructs missing spectral information in latent space before peptide prediction, yielding large reported gains on three benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper studies vaccination decisions in a Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible model, where individuals can become susceptible again after infection. The objective is to shorten an outbreak's extinction time. Unlike approaches that assume the contact graph is known, this work considers an unknown graph and access only to observations of which vertices are infected.

The authors divide the problem into recovering the graph and choosing vaccination strategies. They introduce a graph-learning algorithm based on inclusion-exclusion and establish its sample complexity, quantifying the observations needed for recovery. For vaccination, they address spectral radius minimization, an optimization problem closely connected to effective outbreak control and known to be NP-hard in general.

Their exact algorithm solves spectral radius minimization optimally in polynomial time for graphs with bounded treewidth. For arbitrary graphs, they also provide a polynomial-time greedy heuristic. This distinguishes the conditional optimality result from the more broadly applicable heuristic. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data numerically validate both the graph-learning and vaccination components.
icml-2025-learn-to-vaccinate-combining-s.tldr: The paper learns an unknown infection graph and develops vaccination algorithms, including an optimal polynomial-time method for bounded-treewidth graphs.

paragraphs: Drug-generation models often use docking scores to steer the search for compounds, yet high docking scores do not consistently translate into experimental activity. More accurate computational assessments, including binding free energy calculations based on molecular dynamics, are expensive. MF-LAL addresses the tension between inexpensive guidance and more informative but costly evaluations.

The framework combines several evaluation oracles with different cost-accuracy tradeoffs. Through active learning, it trains a surrogate for each oracle and uses those predictions to guide compound generation. It brings the generator and the multiple surrogate models into one framework, allowing activity prediction and sample generation to be learned together.

Experiments involving two disease-relevant proteins report substantially better binding free energy scores than competing single- and multi-fidelity approaches, including a 50% improvement in the mean score. The reported outcome is an improvement in this computational measure of binding, matching the paper's evaluation. Its broader contribution is a way to incorporate expensive sources of guidance into generation through jointly learned approximations.
icml-2025-mf-lal-drug-compound-generatio.tldr: MF-LAL jointly learns a compound generator and surrogates for multiple evaluation methods, reporting improved binding free energy scores on two protein targets.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces the numerical precision of model weights to make large language models easier to deploy. This paper studies a security risk in which a model appears benign at full precision but exhibits malicious behavior after quantization. Earlier attacks addressed simpler rounding schemes; this work extends the threat to the more complex GGUF family.

The authors exploit quantization error, the difference between original weights and their quantized-and-restored values. Their attack trains a malicious target model while constraining its weights according to those errors. The central finding is that the discrepancy introduced by quantization provides enough flexibility for different behavior to emerge in the deployed, lower-precision model.

The attack is evaluated on three language models, nine GGUF data types, and scenarios involving insecure code generation, targeted content injection, and refusal of benign instructions. The reported deltas are 88.7%, 85.0%, and 30.1%, respectively. These experiments show susceptibility in the tested configurations and support the conclusion that quantization complexity alone is insufficient protection against this form of manipulation.
icml-2025-mind-the-gap-a-practical-attac.tldr: The paper demonstrates attacks that hide malicious behavior at full precision and reveal it after GGUF quantization.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts models are difficult to deploy because of their parameter counts and computational demands. MxMoE starts from two observations: different linear blocks tolerate quantization differently, and experts are activated at different frequencies. These differences mean that choosing numerical precision involves both prediction quality and the way computation is distributed across experts.

The framework selects mixed-precision configurations by considering parameter sensitivity, expert activation patterns, and hardware resources together. It also generates optimized GroupGEMM kernels that run matrix multiplications with different precisions in parallel. This connects the numerical choices made for accuracy with the implementation needed to realize their performance benefits.

Evaluations report Wikitext-2 perplexity 2.4 lower than GPTQ at 2.25-bit precision. They also report speedups of up to 3.4 times over full precision and up to 29.4% over uniform quantization at equivalent accuracy with five-bit weight-activation quantization. These are distinct reported comparisons, supporting the value of coordinating precision selection with hardware execution rather than treating quantization solely as weight compression.
icml-2025-mxmoe-mixed-precision-quantiza.tldr: MxMoE jointly optimizes mixed precision and GPU execution for Mixture-of-Experts models, improving reported accuracy and inference speed.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training examples. Retraining can be expensive, while cheaper approximate methods may fail to reproduce the accuracy and confidence behavior of exact unlearning on forgotten and unseen data. AMUN targets that mismatch by using adversarial examples to adjust how a classifier behaves around the samples to be forgotten.

The method fine-tunes the model on adversarial examples corresponding to forget samples, lowering confidence on those samples. It uses the closest corresponding adversarial examples to keep decision-boundary changes local. The stated rationale is that localized changes can reduce the model's confidence near forgotten examples while avoiding drastic changes to its overall behavior and preserving test accuracy.

The paper reports improvements over prior state-of-the-art image-classification unlearning methods. When forgetting a random 10% of CIFAR-10 samples, the evaluated state-of-the-art membership inference attacks perform no better than random guessing. That empirical result concerns the stated dataset, forgetting setup, and attacks; it provides evidence of reduced membership detectability in that setting.
icml-2025-not-all-wrong-is-bad-using-adv.tldr: AMUN uses nearby adversarial examples to reduce confidence on forgotten samples while preserving test accuracy, with strong reported membership-inference results.

paragraphs: Neural-network normalization often controls the mean and variance of activations, but these quantities do not specify the full shape of their distribution. This paper asks what distribution internal representations should have and how training can encourage it. The authors take inspiration from the information-theoretic properties of the normal, or Gaussian, distribution.

They introduce normality normalization, a layer that uses a power transform to encourage Gaussian-shaped feature representations. It also adds Gaussian noise during training. The proposal therefore gives normalization an explicit distributional target, extending the focus beyond controlling activation averages and variation to shaping the representations themselves.

Experiments report effective generalization across a range of commonly used model and dataset combinations. The method also performs strongly as model width, depth, and training minibatch size vary, and the authors report suitability wherever conventional normalization layers are used. Improved robustness to random perturbations is another stated result. Together, these findings support studying representation shape as a practical component of network normalization.
icml-2025-on-the-importance-of-gaussiani.tldr: Normality normalization encourages Gaussian feature distributions and reports improved generalization and robustness across varied models and training settings.

paragraphs: In partially observable environments, the latest observation may not provide enough information for a reinforcement-learning agent. Past observations matter, but learning from an explicit window becomes increasingly difficult as that window grows. This paper proposes memory traces as a compact way to carry information from observation history into learning.

Inspired by eligibility traces, memory traces summarize observations using exponential moving averages. The authors establish sample complexity bounds for offline on-policy evaluation, quantifying errors in estimated returns for Lipschitz-continuous value estimates. This gives a theoretical account of learning from the compressed history within a specified class of value functions.

The analysis also connects memory traces to observation windows and shows that traces can be significantly more sample efficient in certain environments. That advantage is conditional on the environment, rather than a universal replacement guarantee for windows. Online experiments additionally demonstrate effectiveness for both value prediction and control. The combined results make compact historical summaries a theoretically and empirically supported option for partially observable learning.
icml-2025-partially-observable-reinforce.tldr: Memory traces compress observation histories into exponential moving averages, with evaluation guarantees and sample-efficiency advantages in certain environments.

paragraphs: Designing an enzyme for a specified molecule is particularly difficult when no enzyme is known to catalyze that target. There is no direct enzyme-target supervision for training a generator. This paper addresses that zero-shot setting by drawing on existing enzyme-substrate relationships involving molecules structurally similar to the desired substrate.

The method retrieves enzymes associated with those related substrates, using structural similarity as a source of relevant catalytic information. None of the retrieved enzymes directly catalyze the target molecule. A conditioned discrete diffusion model uses these examples to generate new enzyme sequences, while an enzyme-substrate relationship classifier guides the generation toward suitable sequence distributions.

Evaluations across diverse real-world substrates report better catalytic capability, foldability, and docking accuracy than existing protein-generation methods. The paper also defines the zero-shot substrate-specified generation task and introduces a dataset with evaluation benchmarks. Its contribution combines a concrete design method with a shared evaluation setting for generating enzymes when direct examples for the requested substrate are unavailable.
icml-2025-retrieval-augmented-zero-shot-.tldr: The method retrieves enzymes for structurally related substrates to guide zero-shot enzyme generation for a target without known catalysts.

paragraphs: Bayesian inverse problems use observations to infer an underlying object while accounting for prior knowledge about plausible solutions. This paper builds on work that uses pretrained diffusion models to supply that prior. Its focus is linear-Gaussian inverse problems, giving the proposed inference method a specific mathematical setting.

The authors introduce Decoupled Diffusion Sequential Monte Carlo, or DDSMC. It combines a sequential Monte Carlo method with decoupled diffusion, whose generative process allows larger updates to a sample. The contribution connects that alternative diffusion process with Bayesian inference, using the pretrained generative model within a procedure for solving the inverse problem.

DDSMC is asymptotically exact, a convergence property rather than a claim of exact results from every finite computation. The authors demonstrate its effectiveness on synthetic data and on protein and image data. They also show how the approach can be extended to discrete data. These findings establish both the method's stated inference property and examples of its use across multiple data types.
icml-2025-solving-linear-gaussian-bayesi.tldr: DDSMC combines decoupled diffusion with sequential Monte Carlo for asymptotically exact inference in linear-Gaussian inverse problems.

paragraphs: Some systems contain relationships among groups of entities that are not naturally captured by pairwise links. Hypergraphs represent such higher-order interactions, but obtaining annotated hypergraph structures can be difficult or impossible. SPHINX learns a latent hypergraph from the final task signal, avoiding the need for direct supervision of those relationships.

The model is differentiable end to end while producing a discrete hypergraph that can be used by modern hypergraph networks. It also avoids additional regularization losses for optimization. These design choices make structure inference part of the task-learning process: the inferred relationships are developed through their usefulness to the final prediction task.

Ablation studies and experiments on four challenging datasets show suitable inferred structures in both transductive and inductive tasks. The authors report that the latent hypergraphs are interpretable and improve final performance, outperforming existing hypergraph-prediction methods. The findings support learning higher-order structure from task feedback when an explicit structural annotation is unavailable.
icml-2025-sphinx-structural-prediction-u.tldr: SPHINX learns interpretable discrete hypergraphs from task feedback, improving prediction without requiring annotated higher-order relationships.

paragraphs: Language models sometimes respond meaningfully to text that people find incomprehensible, including strings encountered in jailbreak prompts. This paper investigates such unnatural language as a source of usable model features. The question is whether these strings carry information that models can exploit beyond an isolated unusual response.

The authors find that features in unnatural language can generalize across different models and tasks during inference. They also fine-tune models on unnatural versions of instruction datasets and report performance comparable to training on natural-language versions. Across various base models, the reported average length-controlled AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate is 49.71.

Their analysis attributes processing of these strings to filtering noise and inferring contextual meaning from the words that remain. This supplies an account of how apparently unreadable inputs can still support meaningful model behavior. Together, the transfer and fine-tuning findings challenge the idea that such behavior is only a defect, identifying usable semantic information in the unnatural-language constructions studied.
icml-2025-unnatural-languages-are-not-bu.tldr: The study finds transferable semantic features in human-unreadable text and comparable instruction-tuning performance using unnatural-language datasets.

paragraphs: Class distribution mismatch occurs when the classes encountered in a target task differ from those represented during training. Earlier methods rely heavily on labeled examples and commonly collect unfamiliar classes into an other category. UCDM addresses this mismatch through classifier training that does not rely on labeled data.

The method randomly samples images and uses a diffusion model to add or remove semantic classes, creating positive-negative training pairs. It supplements these synthesized pairs with real-world examples selected through a confidence-based labeling process. That process repeatedly assigns pseudo-labels to useful examples and incorporates them into training, combining generated supervision with information from unlabeled real data.

Experiments on three datasets report better performance than prior semi-supervised approaches. At 60% mismatch on Tiny-ImageNet, UCDM surpasses OpenMatch, which uses 40 labels per class, by reported margins of 35.1%, 63.7%, and 72.5% for known, unknown, and new classes. The findings show that the proposed synthetic-pair and pseudo-labeling strategy can perform strongly in the evaluated mismatch settings without labeled-data dependence.
icml-2025-unsupervised-learning-for-clas.tldr: UCDM combines diffusion-generated training pairs and confidence-based pseudo-labeling to handle class mismatch without labeled data.

paragraphs: Crystal structures often contain substantial symmetry, yet many generative models describe atoms without constraining their positions or elements through that symmetry. WyckoffDiff instead generates symmetry-based descriptions of crystals. Its representation encodes all symmetry, making symmetry a built-in part of the generated description.

The authors develop a neural-network architecture that makes this representation usable within a discrete generative framework. The model respects symmetry by construction, and its discrete formulation enables fast generation. The paper also introduces Fréchet Wrenformer Distance, an evaluation metric intended to capture symmetry-related aspects of generated materials, so assessment reflects a central feature of the model's design.

WyckoffDiff is benchmarked against recently proposed crystal generators. In a proof-of-concept study, the authors also use it to find new materials below the convex hull of thermodynamic stability. That demonstration connects symmetry-aware generation with a materials-discovery objective. The contribution spans representation, architecture, and evaluation, treating crystal symmetry as a core modeling requirement throughout.
icml-2025-wyckoffdiff-a-generative-diffu.tldr: WyckoffDiff generates symmetry-respecting crystal descriptions and demonstrates a proof-of-concept search for materials below the thermodynamic stability convex hull.
